title: Where to Take Photos in the Tri-Cities: A Photographer's Guide
description: After 20 years photographing the Tri-Cities, here's how I choose where to shoot — the kinds of locations that work, the seasons that surprise people, and why.

hero.heading: Where to Take Photos in the Tri-Cities
hero.imageAlt: Family running through an open golden field at sunset during a Tri-Cities photo session
hero.secondaryImageAlt: Evening light reflecting off the Columbia River during a portrait session in Richland, WA

sections.heading: The Short Answer
paragraphs: The best place to take photos in the Tri-Cities is wherever the light is doing something beautiful at the hour you're shooting. That sounds like a dodge, but it's the most useful thing I can tell you after twenty years here: a stunning location at the wrong time of day makes a flat photograph, and an ordinary field at the right moment makes one you'll hang on your wall.
So instead of handing you a list of addresses, let me tell you how I actually think about this — and what I'd look for if I were you.

sections.heading: It Was Never Really About the Place
paragraphs: When people ask me where we should shoot, what they're usually asking is "how do I make sure these photos turn out?" And the honest answer is that the location matters much less than three other things: the hour, the season, and whether you can relax once you get there.

I've learned to hunt for light. Wherever I'm standing, that's what my eyes are doing — reading where it's falling, where it's about to fall, what it's bouncing off of. Photography has genuinely taught me how to see. I'll be out walking at sunrise and notice the way the light catches only the tips of the leaves on a tree, and I take it as a gift — a reminder to find beauty wherever I am and whatever I'm walking through.
That's the skill you're hiring. Not a list of pretty backdrops.
sections.imageAlt: Couple in a small pocket of golden light just before sunset in Kennewick

sections.heading: The Four Kinds of Locations That Work Here
sections.intro: The Tri-Cities gives us a specific palette to work with: dry air, low hills, wide horizons and a river running through the middle of it. That combination makes for exceptionally warm evening light. Almost everything I shoot falls into one of four categories.

items.heading: Open fields and big sky
paragraphs: Grasses that turn gold, hills in the distance, nothing cluttering the background. This is my most-used kind of location, and the reason is practical: your family can move. Walk, run, pile on top of each other, be chased — and the background stays clean the whole time. Busy backgrounds fall apart the moment anybody takes three steps.
items.imageAlt: Family running through an open golden field at sunset during a Tri-Cities photo session

items.heading: The river
paragraphs: The Columbia gives us water light, which is its own thing entirely — softer, brighter from below, and forgiving on faces. Late in the day it turns to sparkle. There's one park I shoot at where, in the colder months, the sun reaches a certain point and the light coming off the river bounces up through the trees. It is genuinely magic, and it happens for about twenty minutes.
items.imageAlt: Evening light reflecting off the Columbia River during a portrait session in Richland, WA

items.heading: Orchards, blossoms and rows
paragraphs: We're surrounded by agriculture and it's underused. Rows give a photograph depth and lead your eye straight to the people in it. Spring blossoms are the obvious version; late-summer dusty gold is the one people forget about.
items.imageAlt: Senior photographed among orchard rows in late summer near Pasco

items.heading: Brick, murals and small-town texture
paragraphs: For seniors and business owners who want edge rather than open country. During a senior session we'll often bounce between several of these — a park, a garden, the river, a coffee shop — because that variety is half the fun of being seventeen with a photographer for an evening.
items.imageAlt: Business owner photographed against brick in the Tri-Cities

sections.heading: What Makes a Location Right for Your Session

items.heading: Families with young children
paragraphs: Room to move, and a background that doesn't get weird when they use it. I'll take an open field over a spectacular but cramped location every time, because I'm going to give your kids activities rather than ask them to stand still — and the photographs are better for it.
items.imageAlt: Family running through an open golden field at sunset during a Tri-Cities photo session

links.label: activities rather than ask them to stand still

items.heading: Seniors
paragraphs: Variety. We'll usually plan two or three spots close enough together that we're not spending your session time driving. What we choose depends entirely on you: some seniors want green and lush, some want dry and moody, some want brick and city.
items.imageAlt: Senior photographed among orchard rows in late summer near Pasco

items.heading: Couples
paragraphs: Somewhere you can forget I'm there. My favorite sessions of my whole career are couples who stopped performing and started actually enjoying each other's company — and then the sun dropped into that small pocket of perfect light right before it sets. That's the one that gets me every time.
items.imageAlt: Couple in a small pocket of golden light just before sunset in Kennewick

items.heading: Newborns
paragraphs: Your own home, almost always. The nursery you painted, the chair where you feed her, the window with the good morning light. No location in the Tri-Cities will ever mean more to your family than that one. When the season is kind, we can add something outdoors.
items.imageAlt: Family holding a newborn at home in the Tri-Cities

items.heading: Business and branding
paragraphs: Your actual workspace first — it says more about your business than any pretty backdrop. For headshots I bring portable studio equipment to you; I've set up in a clinic waiting room and a spare office and gotten exactly what we needed.
items.imageAlt: Business owner photographed in her workspace in Richland, WA

sections.heading: Season by Season in the Tri-Cities

items.heading: May through October
paragraphs: is peak season here, and it's peak for a reason: long golden evenings, warm air, everything green or gold. Fall books out first — if you want October light, ask me in summer.
items.imageAlt: Family photographed outdoors during peak season in the Tri-Cities

items.heading: March and April
paragraphs: can be genuinely beautiful. Blossoms, fresh green, mild evenings, and a much more open calendar.
items.imageAlt: Senior portrait among spring blossoms in the Tri-Cities

items.heading: November through February
paragraphs: is variable. Some weeks are gray and some weeks hand you a gift.
items.imageAlt: Winter portrait session in rare sunny January light in the Tri-Cities

paragraphs: I photograph year-round. Every year is different here, and I'd rather watch the forecast with you than write off four months of the calendar.
items.imageAlt: Family laughing together during a year-round Tri-Cities portrait session

sections.heading: The Case for a Winter Session
paragraphs: Most people won't consider winter, and I understand why. It's often gloomy here, and cold is harder on little kids.

But here's what I know: you do not need flourishing trees to make a beautiful photograph. You need the right spot at the right moment. I shot a session one December on a rare sunny afternoon — the cowboy session — and the light that day was extraordinary. Bare branches, cold air, and some of the warmest light I've ever worked in.
If you get a sunny winter day in the Tri-Cities, take it. They're not common, and they're stunning.
sections.imageAlt: Winter portrait session in rare sunny January light in the Tri-Cities

sections.heading: Why You Don't Have to Choose
sections.intro: Here's the part I most want you to hear: picking the location is my job, not yours.
paragraphs: You don't need to scout anything or arrive with a plan. What helps me is much simpler — tell me what you're drawn to. I'll send you to my Instagram and ask you to like the scenery that pulls at you. That tells me more than any questionnaire ever could, and from there I'll bring you two or three options with the light already worked out, chosen for your family, your style and the time of year we're shooting.

If there's a place that already means something to you — your land, your grandparents' backyard, the field behind your church — bring me there. Those are some of my favorite sessions. I'll find the light when we arrive.
That's what you're paying me for, and honestly, it's the part I love most.
sections.imageAlt: Family photographed in a meaningful outdoor place in the Columbia Basin
sections.secondaryImageAlt: Couple in a small pocket of golden light just before sunset in Kennewick

links.label: That's what you're paying me for

items.heading: What is the best time of day for outdoor photos?
paragraphs: Golden hour — roughly the last 60 to 90 minutes before sunset. In the Tri-Cities that window is generous in summer and short in winter, and I plan every session down to the minute around it.

items.heading: What's the best time of year for photos in the Tri-Cities?
paragraphs: May through October is peak season, with fall booking first. March and April are lovely and much easier to book. Winter is unpredictable but capable of extraordinary light on a clear day.

items.heading: Can we use a location that's meaningful to our family?
paragraphs: Please do. Personal locations almost always produce better photographs than famous ones, because you're relaxed the moment you arrive.

items.heading: Do I need a permit for photos at Tri-Cities parks?
paragraphs: Rules vary by city and by park, and they change. I handle this as part of planning your session, so it isn't something you need to research.

items.heading: What if the weather turns on our session day?
paragraphs: We talk it through. If the calendar allows, I'll happily move us to better light. If it doesn't, we've made beautiful photographs in worse conditions than you'd expect.

finalCta.heading: Let's Find Your Light
paragraphs: You bring your people. I'll bring twenty years of knowing where the light lands in this valley.
